subject: Science (International GCSE Chemistry and Physics)
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1 (Science Double Award 4SD0)
source: Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1 (and Science Double Award 4SD0) specification

lessons.title: Calorimetry practicals: measuring energy changes in solution and combustion
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a polystyrene cup and a thermometer tell us how much energy a reaction releases?
objectives: Describe simple calorimetry for combustion, displacement, dissolving and neutralisation
Calculate energy transferred using Q = mc delta T
Evaluate sources of error and suggest improvements
successCriteria: All: describe the apparatus and what is measured
Most: calculate the energy change and the energy per mole
Some: evaluate heat loss and suggest improvements for each type of experiment
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: energy in food; Maths: unit conversions
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest reporting of results and error

keywords.def: apparatus used to measure the energy transferred in a reaction
final temperature minus initial temperature
energy needed to raise 1 g (or 1 kg) of a substance by 1 °C
energy change per mole of reactant, in kJ/mol

starter: Bismillah. Define exothermic and endothermic.
Write the word equation for neutralisation.
State the unit of energy.

teach.heading: Four types of calorimetry
bullets: Combustion: burn fuel to heat water in a metal can
Neutralisation: mix acid and alkali in a polystyrene cup
Displacement: zinc powder into copper sulfate solution
Dissolving: salt dissolved in water; measure change
teach.note: Compare the set-ups: neutralisation, displacement and dissolving use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid, thermometer and stirrer. Combustion uses a spirit burner under a copper can of water. Ammonium nitrate dissolving is endothermic (temperature falls); neutralisation, displacement and combustion are exothermic (temperature rises). Safety: eye protection, alcohol burners, corrosive solutions.

head: Type
Apparatus
Measure
rows: temperature rise of water; mass of fuel burned

teach.heading: Calculating the energy transferred
bullets: m: mass of water or solution in g
teach.note: Take the density of dilute solutions as that of water, so 1 cm3 has mass 1 g. Divide Q by moles of limiting reagent to give energy per mole; convert J to kJ. Mark energy change as negative for exothermic reactions (enthalpy change). Use data given in the question for c.

model.problem: 25 cm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 HCl is mixed with 25 cm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 NaOH. The temperature rises by 13.6 °C. Calculate Q and the energy change per mole of water formed. (c = 4.2 J/g °C; 1 cm3 = 1 g)
steps: Moles of HCl = 25/1000 x 2.0 = 0.050 mol
Energy per mole = 2856 / 0.050 = 57 120 J/mol
= about 57 kJ/mol (exothermic, so -57 kJ/mol)

teach.heading: Check: the cup
teach.note: Option A is the idea that a lid does not matter. Option D reverses the effect.

check.q: Why is a lid put on the polystyrene cup?
options: to reduce heat loss to the surroundings
check.why: A lid and polystyrene reduce the heat lost, giving a temperature change closer to the true value.

teach.heading: Evaluating the results
bullets: Heat loss makes the measured rise too small
In combustion most energy escapes to the air
Use a lid, a draught shield and a stirrer
teach.note: The measured value of combustion is much lower than the data-book value because of heat loss. Ask: how can you improve the experiment? (Insulate the can, put a draught shield around, bring the flame closer, stir the water, burn the fuel completely.)

misconception.wrong: The temperature of a reaction mixture shows how much energy was released, with no other factors.
misconception.right: Heat losses and the mass of water also matter. Energy released depends on the temperature change AND the mass of the solution, and heat loss makes the measured value too low.

teach.heading: Practical plan
bullets: Record the initial temperature for a few minutes
Add the second reagent and stir
Record the highest or lowest temperature
teach.note: For dissolving ammonium nitrate record the lowest temperature and for neutralisation record the highest. Plot temperature against time if possible and extrapolate to correct for heat loss.

practice: Calculate Q for 100 g water heated through 8.0 °C (c = 4.2 J/g °C).
Explain why a polystyrene cup is used.
State whether dissolving ammonium nitrate is exothermic or endothermic.
independent: Core: Describe how to measure the temperature change when zinc powder is added to copper sulfate solution.
Extend: A fuel heats 200 g water by 20 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.
Stretch: Compare the measured and data-book energy changes for burning ethanol and explain the difference.
exit: State the equation for Q.
State two ways to improve a combustion experiment.
Big question: how do we measure energy from a reaction?
lessons.homework: Write a plan to compare two fuels using the same apparatus. State the variables to control.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide labelled diagrams and a substitution template. Stretch: explain why extrapolating the cooling curve improves accuracy.

lessons.title: Reversible reactions in practice: hydrated copper(II) sulfate and ammonium chloride
lessons.bigQuestion: Which solid changes from blue to white and back again, and which vanishes when heated but reappears elsewhere?
objectives: Describe the reversible dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate
Describe the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride and its reversal
Write equations using the reversible arrow
successCriteria: All: state the colour changes of copper(II) sulfate
Most: write the equations for both reversible reactions
Some: explain the observations including the movement of the gases
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry in industry: drying agents; Geology: hydrated minerals
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the cycles in nature

keywords.def: a reaction where products can react to form the original reactants
containing water of crystallisation
without water of crystallisation
breakdown of a compound by heat

starter: Bismillah. Define a reversible reaction.
State the symbol used for a reversible reaction.
Describe a test for water.

teach.heading: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate
bullets: Heat strongly: steam given off, white powder remains
Add water to the white solid: it turns blue and gets hot
teach.note: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O (blue) reversible reaction CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O. Heating drives off the water (endothermic); adding water is exothermic and regenerates the blue colour. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is used as a test for water but does not show that water is pure. Do not heat the crystals above a gentle flame; the test tube should be held at an angle with the mouth pointing away.

teach.heading: Equation practice
teach.note: Practise writing the equation. Check pupils put the 5 in front of H2O only, and treat the dot as 'with' water.

model.problem: Write the equation for the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate and describe what you see.
steps: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is CuSO4.5H2O
Heating releases water as steam
CuSO4.5H2O(s) reversible CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(g)
Blue crystals turn to a white powder
model.answer: CuSO4.5H2O(s) reversible CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(g); blue to white

teach.heading: Ammonium chloride
bullets: Heat white ammonium chloride in a test tube
It decomposes to ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases
The gases rise, cool and recombine
White solid forms again on the cooler upper part of the tube
teach.note: Equation: NH4Cl(s) reversible NH3(g) + HCl(g). Damp red litmus paper at the mouth turns blue first (ammonia), and then red or blue-to-red as hydrogen chloride arrives, because ammonia diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride (it is lighter). Do this as a demonstration in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated space. Pupils should explain that the solid seems to 'sublime' but in fact is decomposing and recombining.
cycle: Heat the white solid ammonium chloride
It decomposes to NH3 and HCl gases
The gases rise up the cooler tube
White solid ring forms on the upper tube

teach.heading: Check: observations
teach.note: Option B shows the idea that the solid sublimes. Option C reverses the colour change.

check.q: What is seen when anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is added to water?
check.why: The white powder rehydrates, turns blue and the mixture warms up.

teach.heading: Why this matters
bullets: Reversible reactions can go either way
Used in the Haber process later
teach.note: Link to dynamic equilibrium in the existing lesson: in an open test tube the steam escapes, so the reverse reaction is not possible; in a closed system a mixture reaches equilibrium.

practice: State the colour of hydrated copper(II) sulfate.
Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride.
Explain why a white solid appears near the top of the tube.
independent: Core: Describe what you see when blue copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated and then cooled with water added.
Extend: Write balanced equations with state symbols for both reactions.
Stretch: Explain why the products of ammonium chloride decomposition separate and can be identified with litmus.
exit: State what 'anhydrous' means.
Write the symbol for a reversible reaction.
Big question: describe one reaction that goes both ways.
lessons.homework: Write a short explanation of how ammonium chloride seems to disappear and reappear.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a photo sequence and colour cards. Stretch: link to why sealed vessels allow equilibrium.

lessons.title: Homologous series, functional groups and isomers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do chemists have so many compounds with similar names and similar formulae?
objectives: Define homologous series, functional group and isomerism
Recognise members of a homologous series from formulae
Draw and name isomers of simple alkanes
successCriteria: All: say what a homologous series is
Most: identify a functional group and general formula
Some: draw and name all the isomers of C5H12 and C4H8
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order and pattern in creation

keywords.def: a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH2
the atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties
compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
the formula that applies to all members of a series

starter: Bismillah. Name the first four alkanes.
State the general formula of the alkanes.
Draw the displayed formula of ethene.

teach.heading: Homologous series
bullets: Similar chemical properties; physical properties change gradually
teach.note: Examples: alkanes CnH2n+2 (C-C single bonds), alkenes CnH2n (C=C), alcohols CnH2n+1OH (-OH), carboxylic acids CnH2n+1COOH (-COOH). Physical properties such as boiling point increase with the chain length. Ask pupils to give the formula of the next member after C3H8 (C4H10).

teach.heading: Functional groups
bullets: The rest of the molecule matters less
teach.note: Link to prior knowledge: bromine water test for C=C. A functional group is the reactive centre of the molecule, so members of a series react in similar ways. Ask: what is the functional group in ethanol?

misconception.wrong: Isomers are the same molecule drawn in a different way.
misconception.right: Isomers are different compounds with the same molecular formula. They have different structures and often different properties. A different drawing of the same chain is not an isomer.

teach.heading: Isomers
bullets: Branched isomers have lower boiling points
teach.note: Show the carbon skeletons: butane CH3CH2CH2CH3 and 2-methylpropane (CH3)2CHCH3. For C5H12: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane. Branched isomers have lower boiling points because they have less surface contact between molecules (weaker intermolecular forces). Tip: do not count rotations or flips of the same chain as new isomers.

model.problem: Draw and name the isomers of C4H10.
steps: Longest chain of 4 carbons: butane CH3CH2CH2CH3
Chain of 3 carbons with a CH3 branch on carbon 2: 2-methylpropane
Check both have formula C4H10
No other arrangement is possible

teach.heading: Check: isomers
teach.note: Option A has the same molecular formula and the same structure, so is not an isomer; Option C has a different formula.

check.why: Both are C4H10 but have different arrangements of atoms. The others are the same molecule or have different formulae.

teach.heading: Isomers in alkenes
bullets: The double bond is in a different position
Numbers show the position of the functional group
teach.note: For C4H8 the structural isomers are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene (cyclic isomers are beyond the spec). Position isomers differ in where the C=C is, so the number in the name matters.

practice: State the general formula of the alkenes.
Give the molecular formula of the next member after C3H7OH.
Explain why butane and 2-methylpropane are isomers.
independent: Core: Complete a table of the first four members of the alkanes with formulae.
Extend: Draw the three isomers of C5H12 and name them.
Stretch: Explain why a branched isomer has a lower boiling point than the straight-chain isomer.
exit: Define a functional group.
Draw one isomer of C4H10 that is not butane.
Big question: how can two compounds have the same formula but be different?
lessons.homework: Make a one-page poster on the four homologous series in the course, with a general formula and an example for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide molecular model pictures to compare isomers. Stretch: discuss why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.

lessons.title: Alcohols: names, oxidation and why fermentation needs no air
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does an ethanol solution turn to vinegar if it is left open to the air?
objectives: Name and write formulae for methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol
Describe three ways ethanol can be oxidised
Explain why fermentation needs no air and has an optimum temperature
successCriteria: All: name and write formulae for the first four alcohols
Most: state the products of oxidation of ethanol and the dichromate colour change
Some: explain the conditions for fermentation using enzymes and oxygen
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: respiration in yeast; Food technology: vinegar
lessons.smsc: Moral: understanding why Islam prohibits drinking alcohol, while chemistry studies ethanol as a fuel and solvent

keywords.def: organic compound containing the -OH functional group
gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen)
anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast to ethanol and carbon dioxide
temperature at which a reaction or enzyme works best

starter: Bismillah. Write the general formula of the alcohols.
State the functional group of an alcohol.
State what an enzyme is.

teach.heading: The first four alcohols
teach.note: Paper 2 only: this lesson covers separate Chemistry (4CH1) content, not Double Award. General formula CnH2n+1OH. The number in propan-1-ol shows that the -OH is on the first carbon. Ask pupils to draw displayed formulae. Methanol is toxic, a reminder to never taste laboratory chemicals.

teach.heading: Three ways to oxidise ethanol
bullets: Burning in air: carbon dioxide and water
Heat with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): ethanoic acid
teach.note: Equations: C2H5OH + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 3H2O; C2H5OH + O2 gives CH3COOH + H2O (microbial oxidation by bacteria in air, which turns ethanol solutions sour); with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) the orange solution turns green as dichromate is reduced. The mixture is heated under reflux so that vapour is condensed and returned. Remember that dichromate(VI) is toxic and a carcinogen (teacher demonstration).
cycle: Add oxidising agent or bacteria with air

teach.heading: Fermentation conditions
bullets: No air: oxygen would give aerobic respiration or oxidise the ethanol
teach.note: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration by yeast. If air is present, yeast respire aerobically producing carbon dioxide and water, and bacteria may oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid. Too cold: slow reaction because enzymes have low kinetic energy; too hot (above about 45 °C, approx.): enzymes are denatured and the yeast die. Use an airlock to let carbon dioxide escape but not let air in. Optimum around 35 °C (verify against the specification wording).

model.problem: Explain why a brewer keeps the fermentation vessel sealed and at about 35 °C.
steps: Without oxygen, yeast produce ethanol and carbon dioxide (anaerobic)
Air would allow oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid
35 °C is near the optimum for yeast enzymes
Too high a temperature denatures the enzymes
model.answer: No air stops oxidation; the optimum temperature gives the fastest reaction without denaturing enzymes.

teach.heading: Check: oxidation
teach.note: Option B is the product of reduction. Option D is the common error of naming ethanal instead of ethanoic acid for the final product.

check.q: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is heated with ethanol. What colour change is seen?
check.why: Dichromate(VI) is orange and is reduced to green chromium(III) as the ethanol is oxidised.

practice: Write the formula of propan-1-ol.
Write the word equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
State why fermentation is carried out without air.
independent: Core: Draw displayed formulae for methanol and ethanol.
Extend: Write balanced equations for the burning of ethanol and for its microbial oxidation.
Stretch: Explain why an ethanol solution left open goes sour and why a fermenter needs temperature control.
exit: Name the functional group in alcohols.
State the colour change in the dichromate test.
Big question: what happens to an ethanol solution left open and why?
lessons.homework: Write the equation for fermentation and explain two conditions needed.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide displayed formula templates and sequencing cards. Stretch: link to enzyme denaturation.

lessons.title: Carboxylic acid reactions and esters: smells, uses and preparation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a rotten pineapple smell so different from vinegar, yet they are chemically related?
objectives: Describe the reactions of carboxylic acid solutions with metals and carbonates
State properties and uses of esters
Describe how to prepare ethyl ethanoate
successCriteria: All: write the word equations for the reactions of ethanoic acid
Most: describe the properties and uses of esters and the preparation steps
Some: write balanced symbol equations and explain each step in the preparation

keywords.def: organic acid containing the -COOH group
compound formed when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid
evaporates easily
speeds up a reaction without being used up

starter: Bismillah. State the formula and functional group of ethanoic acid.
State what an acid and a metal produce.
State the test for carbon dioxide.

teach.heading: Acid reactions of carboxylic acids
bullets: With a reactive metal: salt and hydrogen
With a carbonate: salt, water and carbon dioxide
Reactions are slower than with strong acids
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Chemistry (4CH1) content. Equations: 2CH3COOH + Mg gives (CH3COO)2Mg + H2; 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 gives 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, so it ionises only partly, so fizzing is gentler than with hydrochloric acid. Pupils can test for hydrogen (squeaky pop) and carbon dioxide (limewater milky).

teach.heading: Making an ester
bullets: Ethanol + ethanoic acid gives ethyl ethanoate + water
Add a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid
Warm gently in a hot water bath
Pour into sodium carbonate solution and smell
teach.note: Equation: C2H5OH + CH3COOH reversible CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. Concentrated sulfuric acid is a catalyst and is corrosive; wear eye protection. Use a hot water bath, not a naked flame, as ethanol and the ester are flammable. Sodium carbonate solution neutralises excess acid so the fruity smell of the ester can be detected. The ester forms a separate layer on top of the aqueous solution.
cycle: Add a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid
Warm in a hot water bath

teach.heading: Properties and uses of esters
bullets: Strong, often sweet or fruity smells
teach.note: Esters are the reason fruits and flowers smell as they do. Natural and artificial flavourings can contain esters. Names follow alcohol + acid: ethyl (from ethanol) ethanoate (from ethanoic acid). Ask: what ester forms from methanol and ethanoic acid? (methyl ethanoate)

model.problem: Name the ester formed from propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid, and state one use of esters.
steps: The alcohol part gives the first word: propyl
The acid part gives the second word: ethanoate
Name: propyl ethanoate
Esters are used in perfumes and food flavourings
model.answer: Propyl ethanoate; used as flavourings or perfumes

teach.heading: Check: carboxylic acid with carbonate
teach.note: Option C omits water, a common slip. Option D forgets that carbonates produce carbon dioxide, not hydrogen.

check.q: Which products form when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate?
options: sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
sodium ethanoate and carbon dioxide only
check.why: Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide. Hydrogen comes from metals.

teach.heading: Safety and evaluation
teach.note: Discuss why the reaction does not go to completion (reversible). Removing water or adding excess alcohol can increase the yield; mention only if pupils ask.

practice: Write the word equation for ethanoic acid reacting with magnesium.
Name the ester made from methanol and propanoic acid.
State the role of concentrated sulfuric acid in ester preparation.
independent: Core: Describe how to prepare ethyl ethanoate with a safety note.
Extend: Write balanced equations for ethanoic acid reacting with calcium carbonate.
Stretch: Explain why the esterification reaction does not give a 100% yield.
exit: Name the group in a carboxylic acid.
State one use of an ester.
Big question: how are vinegar and fruity smells related?
lessons.homework: Find three esters in food or perfume ingredient lists and write the alcohol and acid for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide naming cards (alcohol + acid). Stretch: explain why esters have lower boiling points than the acids from which they are made (no hydrogen bonding; verify).

lessons.title: Pressure difference in a liquid and the units of pressure
lessons.bigQuestion: Why must a submarine hull be stronger the deeper it dives?
objectives: State the units for pressure, density, length, area, volume, force, speed and acceleration
Calculate the pressure difference between two depths using delta p = h x rho x g
Explain why pressure increases with depth
successCriteria: All: state the units used with pressure and density
Most: calculate the pressure difference for a given depth
Some: calculate the pressure difference between two points and relate it to a real situation
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: ocean depths; Engineering: dams and submarines
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the depths of the oceans

keywords.def: force per unit area, in pascals
mass per unit volume, in kg/m3
vertical distance below the surface
unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m2

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for pressure in terms of force and area.
Calculate the pressure from a 60 N force on 0.30 m2.
State the equation for density.

teach.heading: Units used in this topic
bullets: Energy: J; mass: kg; density: kg/m3
Length: m; area: m2; volume: m3
Force: N; pressure: Pa; speed m/s; acceleration m/s2
teach.note: Quick-fire. Convert: 1 cm3 = 1 x 10 to the power -6 m3; 1 g/cm3 = 1000 kg/m3; 1 cm2 = 1 x 10 to the power -4 m2. 1 Pa = 1 N/m2. Temperature changes in °C and K are the same size; absolute temperature in K = °C + 273.

teach.heading: Pressure in a liquid
bullets: Increases with depth and with density
Due to the weight of the liquid above
Pressure difference = h x rho x g
teach.note: Pressure difference between two levels: delta p = h rho g where h is the vertical height between them in m, rho the density in kg/m3 and g the gravitational field strength in N/kg. Pressure depends on vertical depth only, not on the shape of the container. The deep-sea or dam wall are thicker at the base. g = 10 N/kg is used here; use the value given.

model.problem: A diver is 20 m below the surface of sea water (density 1030 kg/m3). Calculate the pressure difference between the surface and the diver. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: delta p = h rho g
delta p = 20 x 1030 x 10
delta p = 206 000 Pa
Atmospheric pressure (about 100 000 Pa) acts too, so total about 306 000 Pa
model.answer: 206 000 Pa (2.06 x 10 to the power 5 Pa)

teach.heading: Check: depth
teach.note: Option B reverses the effect. Option D is the idea that volume of water matters.

check.q: A submarine dives from 50 m to 150 m. What happens to the pressure on the hull?
options: it increases by delta p = 100 x rho x g
it depends on the width of the ocean
check.why: Pressure difference depends on the vertical depth change of 100 m, the density and g.

teach.heading: Difference between two points
bullets: Use the vertical height between the points
Not the total depth if both are underwater
A dam is thicker at the bottom
Water towers use height to give pressure
teach.note: Ask: what is the pressure difference between points 5 m and 20 m deep in a lake (density 1000 kg/m3)? h = 15 m so delta p = 15 x 1000 x 10 = 150 000 Pa. A water tower on a hill gives pressure at the tap because of the height of water above.

practice: State the unit of pressure and its equivalent in N and m2.
Calculate the pressure difference for 8.0 m of water (1000 kg/m3, g = 10 N/kg).
Explain why the base of a dam is thicker.
independent: Core: Calculate the pressure difference for three depths in sea water.
Extend: Calculate the pressure difference between 5 m and 25 m in a lake.
Stretch: Mercury has a density of 13 600 kg/m3. Calculate the height of a mercury column that gives a pressure of 100 000 Pa (g = 10 N/kg).
exit: State the equation for pressure difference in a liquid.
Calculate delta p for h = 12 m, rho = 1000 kg/m3, g = 10 N/kg.
Big question: why does a submarine need a strong hull?
lessons.homework: Look up the greatest depth of the Mariana Trench (about 11 km; verify) and estimate the pressure difference from the surface.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a formula triangle with units. Stretch: explain why pressure at a point acts equally in all directions.

lessons.title: Gas molecules and temperature, and the unit J/kg °C
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a sealed can of gas become dangerous in a hot car?
objectives: Explain that a higher temperature raises the average speed of gas molecules
Link molecular speed to gas pressure at constant volume
Use the unit J/kg °C for specific heat capacity (Paper 2 only)
successCriteria: All: state that hotter gas molecules move faster
Most: explain the rise in pressure using collisions
Some: use the specific heat capacity unit consistently in calculations
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: collision theory; Safety: aerosol cans

keywords.def: gas particles move randomly and collide with surfaces to produce pressure
lowest possible temperature, 0 K
unit of absolute temperature; K = °C + 273
energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C, in J/kg °C

starter: Bismillah. Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
Describe the arrangement of particles in a gas.
State why gas pressure acts on the walls of a container.

teach.heading: Temperature and molecular speed
bullets: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles
Higher temperature: molecules move faster on average
Not every molecule has the same speed
At 0 K particles have minimum energy
teach.note: Draw a Maxwell-style speed distribution only as a sketch: the curve shifts to higher speeds at higher temperature, but the key idea is average speed. Convert °C to K by adding 273. Avoid saying 'all molecules speed up equally'. Link to the previous lesson on the Kelvin scale and gas pressure.

teach.heading: Explaining pressure changes
bullets: More frequent and harder collisions with the walls
teach.note: Use the three-step explanation: faster, more often, harder. Each collision exerts a force; pressure is total force per area. Ask: why do aerosol cans warn against heating? Because the pressure can rise enough to burst the can.

model.problem: Explain why the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container rises when it is heated.
steps: Heating gives the molecules more kinetic energy so they move faster
They hit the walls more often
Each collision has a greater force
The total force per unit area increases, so pressure rises
model.answer: Faster molecules collide more often and harder with the walls, increasing pressure.

teach.heading: Check: kinetic theory
teach.note: Option A is the typical idea that molecules expand. Option C misses that only the average speed rises.

check.q: A gas is heated in a rigid container. Which statement is correct?
options: the average speed of the molecules increases
all the molecules move at the same speed
check.why: A higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy and therefore speed, not bigger particles or more of them.

teach.heading: The unit J/kg °C
bullets: Energy in J, mass in kg, temperature change in °C
Higher c: more energy needed to warm the same mass
teach.note: Paper 2 only: the unit is flagged as separate Physics (4PH1) content. Link to the specific heat capacity lesson. Check the units: J / (kg x °C). Calculation: 0.50 kg of water heated by 20 °C needs 0.50 x 4200 x 20 = 42 000 J.

model.problem: How much energy is needed to heat 0.50 kg of water by 20 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg °C)
steps: E = m c delta T
Unit check: kg x J/kg °C x °C = J

practice: Convert 100 °C to kelvin.
Explain why gas pressure rises when the temperature rises at constant volume.
Calculate the energy needed to heat 2.0 kg of water by 5.0 °C (c = 4200 J/kg °C).
independent: Core: Write a three-step explanation of why pressure rises on heating.
Extend: Calculate the energy to heat 1.5 kg of oil by 30 °C (c = 2000 J/kg °C).
Stretch: Explain what happens to the average speed of the molecules at absolute zero and why pressure falls to zero in the model.
exit: State what happens to average molecular speed when temperature rises.
State the unit of specific heat capacity.
Big question: why is a hot car dangerous for a sealed spray can?
lessons.homework: Make a labelled diagram of gas particles in a cool and a hot container and write a three-sentence explanation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a slow-motion particle animation and a sentence frame (faster, more often, harder). Stretch: relate the speed distribution to evaporation.

lessons.title: Building an electromagnet and the units A, V and W
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a scrapyard crane pick up a car and then let go?
objectives: State the units A, V and W
Describe the construction of an electromagnet
Explain how to increase the strength of an electromagnet
successCriteria: All: describe a solenoid with an iron core
Most: list three ways to increase strength and explain why soft iron is used
Some: plan an investigation of electromagnet strength with controlled variables
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: scrapyard cranes, relays and bells; Design technology
lessons.smsc: Social: using technology to serve people

keywords.def: a magnet created by an electric current in a coil
a long coil of wire
iron that magnetises easily and loses magnetism when the current stops
the material inside the coil

starter: Bismillah. Draw the magnetic field around a bar magnet.
State what is produced around a wire carrying a current.
State the equation for electrical power.

teach.heading: Units: ampere, volt, watt
teach.note: Quick check: a 12 V supply drives 3.0 A through a coil: P = 12 x 3.0 = 36 W. Remind pupils to use the correct units in each calculation. Link to the earlier electrical units lesson.

teach.heading: Construction of an electromagnet
bullets: Insulated copper wire wound into a coil (solenoid)
Soft iron core inside the coil
Direct current from a cell or power supply
Switch to turn the field on and off
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. Insulated wire stops the current taking shortcuts between turns. Soft iron is magnetised by the coil field, so the total field is much stronger, but it loses its magnetism when the current is switched off. Steel would stay magnetised, so cannot be switched off. Uses: cranes in scrapyards, relays, electric bells, door locks.

teach.heading: Making it stronger
teach.note: Test by counting how many paperclips are picked up. Control variables: same coil, same length of wire and the same nail. Increasing current heats the wire, so use short measurement times and take care. Ask pupils to plan the investigation and name the independent, dependent and control variables.

model.problem: A student wants to show how the number of turns affects the strength of an electromagnet. Describe the plan.
steps: Independent variable: number of turns (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40)
Dependent variable: number of paperclips picked up
Control: same current, same iron nail, same type of wire
Repeat three times and calculate the mean
model.answer: The more turns, the more paperclips are picked up.

teach.heading: Check: strength
teach.note: Option B would reduce the strength. Option C is a plausible but incorrect idea, since a plastic core does not concentrate the field.

check.q: Which change does NOT make an electromagnet stronger?
options: a plastic core instead of iron
check.why: A plastic core is not magnetic and does not strengthen the field.

practice: State the unit of power.
Calculate the power when 9.0 V drives a 2.0 A current through a coil.
Explain why soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet.
independent: Core: Draw and label an electromagnet.
Extend: Describe two uses of electromagnets and explain why an electromagnet is better than a permanent magnet in each.
Stretch: Explain why increasing the current has a limit in practice.
exit: List three ways to strengthen an electromagnet.
State why the wire is insulated.
Big question: how does a crane drop the car?
lessons.homework: Build or sketch an electromagnet with a nail and wire and describe how you would test it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled diagram and variable sorting cards. Stretch: explain how a relay uses a small current to switch a large one.

lessons.title: The transformer: structure and power in equals power out
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a phone charger change 230 V into a safe 5 V?
objectives: Describe the structure of a transformer
Use the turns ratio to calculate output voltage
Use VpIp = VsIs for a transformer that is 100% efficient
successCriteria: All: label the primary coil, secondary coil and iron core
Most: calculate the voltage from the turns and explain why a.c. is needed
Some: calculate currents for an ideal transformer and explain the benefit for power transmission
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: the National Grid; Technology: chargers
lessons.smsc: Social: providing safe, shared electricity to communities

keywords.def: device that changes the size of an alternating voltage
the input coil
the output coil
transformer that increases the voltage

starter: Bismillah. State what electromagnetic induction is.
State the equation for electrical power.
Explain why transmission uses high voltage.

teach.heading: Structure of a transformer
bullets: Wound on a laminated soft iron core
Primary coil: input; secondary coil: output
The core links the magnetic field between the coils
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. Alternating current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field in the core. This changing field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary. A direct current does not work because the field does not change. The core is laminated (made of thin sheets) to reduce eddy currents; mention as stretch only (verify). The number of turns decides the output voltage.

teach.heading: Turns ratio
bullets: Ratio of voltages equals ratio of turns
teach.note: Check pupils use the same coil order on both sides. Example: 230 V input, primary of 1150 turns, secondary of 50 turns.

model.problem: A transformer has 1150 turns on the primary coil and 50 turns on the secondary coil. The input is 230 V. Calculate the output voltage.
steps: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Vs = 10 V

teach.heading: Power in equals power out
bullets: Step up the voltage: the current falls
teach.note: Apply it to the previous example: 10 V at 2.0 A secondary is 20 W, so Ip = 20 / 230 = 0.087 A. Real transformers lose some energy as heat, so output power is slightly smaller. High-voltage transmission means lower current in the cables, so less energy is wasted as heat (P = I squared R).

model.problem: The secondary of an ideal transformer delivers 2.0 A at 10 V. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the primary current.
steps: Power out = Vs Is = 10 x 2.0 = 20 W
Power in = power out = 20 W

teach.heading: Check: ideal transformer
teach.note: Option A is a usual error: confusing step-up with the same current. Option D forgets that direct current cannot work.

check.q: A step-up transformer has 100% efficiency. What happens to the current?
check.why: Voltage increases, so for the same power the current must decrease.

teach.heading: Why a.c. only
bullets: d.c. gives a steady field in the core
teach.note: Ask: what would a battery connected to the primary do? Nothing after the first moment, since there would be no changing flux. Link to the earlier electromagnetic induction lesson.

practice: Name the three main parts of a transformer.
A transformer has 200 turns in the primary and 1000 in the secondary. The input is 12 V. Calculate the output voltage.
A step-down transformer is 100% efficient and the input is 230 V at 0.50 A. Calculate the output power.
independent: Core: Label a transformer and describe how it works.
Extend: Calculate the secondary current for an ideal transformer with Vp = 230 V, Ip = 0.20 A, Vs = 23 V.
Stretch: Explain why high voltage transmission reduces energy loss in cables.
exit: State why a transformer needs a.c.
State the power equation for an ideal transformer.
Big question: how does a charger give 5 V from 230 V?
lessons.homework: Look at the label of a phone charger and record the input and output voltages and calculate the turns ratio.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a ratio template and labelled diagram. Stretch: calculate efficiency if the output is 90% of the input power.

lessons.title: Why fusion needs extreme temperature and pressure
lessons.bigQuestion: If fusion powers the Sun, why is it so hard to make on Earth?
objectives: Describe nuclear fusion
Explain that nuclei repel each other because protons are positively charged
Explain why fusion needs high temperature and high pressure
successCriteria: All: describe what fusion is
Most: explain the electrostatic repulsion of nuclei
Some: justify the conditions in the Sun and in fusion reactors
lessons.crossCurricular: Energy engineering; Astronomy: how stars shine
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the Sun as a sign of order and benefit

keywords.def: joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
force pushing apart objects with like charges
a very hot gas of ions and electrons
atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

starter: Bismillah. State the charge on a proton and a neutron.
State the rule for like charges.
Name the process that powers the Sun.

teach.heading: What is fusion?
bullets: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
Powers the Sun and other stars
teach.note: Reaction: hydrogen-2 (deuterium) + hydrogen-3 (tritium) gives helium-4 + a neutron + energy. Check the mass numbers: 2 + 3 = 4 + 1. Check the charge: 1 + 1 = 2 + 0. The mass of the products is very slightly smaller than the reactants; the difference is released as energy (E = mc squared is beyond this specification; do not require it).

teach.heading: The barrier: electrostatic repulsion
bullets: The repulsion grows as nuclei approach
Nuclei must get very close to fuse
teach.note: Analogy: pushing two like magnetic poles together. The nuclei must get very close before the strong nuclear force (very short range) takes over and binds them. Therefore the nuclei need a large amount of kinetic energy to overcome repulsion. Do not use the word 'bonds' for the nuclear force without explanation.

misconception.wrong: Fusion happens easily because nuclei are very small and attract each other.
misconception.right: Nuclei are positively charged and repel strongly. They must be given a lot of kinetic energy to get close enough to fuse.

teach.heading: High temperature and high pressure
bullets: High temperature: nuclei move very fast
Fast nuclei can overcome the repulsion
More frequent collisions give a higher fusion rate
teach.note: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C (approx.; verify), with the huge pressure from gravity. Fusion reactors on Earth need temperatures of roughly 100 million °C or more (approx.) and a magnetic field to confine the plasma, because no material container could survive. Short answer model: high temperature gives enough kinetic energy to overcome repulsion; high pressure brings nuclei close together so collisions are frequent.

model.problem: Explain why nuclear fusion needs a very high temperature and pressure.
steps: Nuclei are positively charged so they repel each other
High temperature gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to get close despite the repulsion
High pressure squeezes nuclei together so collisions are more frequent
So fusion is only possible in stars or specially built reactors
model.answer: High temperature overcomes electrostatic repulsion; high pressure increases collision rate.

teach.heading: Check: fusion
teach.note: Option A is the typical confusion with fission. Option C reverses the effect of temperature.

check.q: Why do nuclei need a lot of kinetic energy to fuse?
options: to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between protons
check.why: Protons repel each other. The nuclei need enough kinetic energy to get close enough to fuse.

practice: State what happens in nuclear fusion.
Explain why nuclei repel each other.
State two conditions needed for fusion.
independent: Core: Complete the fusion equation for deuterium and tritium by balancing the numbers.
Extend: Explain why fusion happens in the Sun but is hard to achieve in a laboratory.
Stretch: Compare fusion and fission in terms of fuel, products and conditions.
exit: State why fusion needs a high temperature.
Name one thing the reactor must do with the plasma.
Big question: why is fusion hard on Earth?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word paragraph explaining why fusion could be a useful source of energy and why it is difficult.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a magnet analogy and a labelled diagram. Stretch: explain magnetic confinement.

lessons.title: The scale of the universe and gravitational field strength
lessons.bigQuestion: How many stars are there, and how heavy would you be on another world?
objectives: State the units kg, m, m/s, m/s2, N, s and N/kg
Describe the hierarchy of planet, star, galaxy and universe
Use W = mg with different gravitational field strengths
successCriteria: All: order the objects by size and state the units
Most: describe the Milky Way and calculate weight on other worlds
Some: compare orders of magnitude and explain why weight varies while mass stays the same
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Earth in space; Maths: standard form
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the vastness of creation and humility

keywords.def: a very large group of stars held together by gravity
the galaxy that contains our Solar System
everything that exists: all space, matter and energy
force per unit mass, in N/kg

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for weight.
Name the force that keeps the planets in orbit.
Write 3 000 000 in standard form.

teach.heading: The hierarchy of the universe
bullets: Solar System: Sun and its orbiting bodies
The Milky Way is our spiral galaxy
teach.note: Use approximate figures with care: the Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars (approx. 100-400 billion; verify) and the observable universe has about two trillion galaxies in some estimates (verify). Say 'billions of galaxies' as in the specification. Distances: a light-year is about 9.5 x 10 to the power 15 m (verify). Our Sun is one ordinary star.

teach.heading: Units in astrophysics
teach.note: N/kg and m/s2 are equivalent for gravitational acceleration. Typical values (approx.; use values given in the exam): Earth 9.8 N/kg, Moon 1.6 N/kg, Mars 3.7 N/kg, Jupiter about 25 N/kg.

teach.heading: Weight on other worlds
bullets: g depends on the body's mass and radius
Weight is a force in newtons
teach.note: Common error: saying mass changes on the Moon. It does not.

model.problem: A 60 kg astronaut stands on the Moon where g = 1.6 N/kg. Calculate the weight. Compare with Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: W = m g
Moon: W = 60 x 1.6 = 96 N
Earth: W = 60 x 10 = 600 N
Mass is 60 kg in both places
model.answer: 96 N on the Moon; 600 N on Earth; mass unchanged

teach.heading: Check: mass and weight
teach.note: Option A is the main misconception. Option C swaps units.

check.q: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. Which quantity stays the same?
check.why: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. Weight changes because g changes.

practice: Put in order from smallest to largest: galaxy, planet, universe, star.
Calculate the weight of a 2.0 kg object on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg).
State the unit of gravitational field strength.
independent: Core: Complete the hierarchy table of the universe with an example of each.
Extend: Calculate the weight of a 50 kg person on the Earth, Moon and Jupiter.
Stretch: Jupiter has a much larger g than Earth. Explain what this tells you about the force on a 1 kg mass there and how its weight would compare.
exit: Name the galaxy that contains our Sun.
State why mass does not change on the Moon.
Big question: how heavy would you be on another world?
lessons.homework: Write a postcard from another planet explaining your weight and why your mass did not change.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a size-order card sort. Stretch: explain how standard form helps with large numbers.

lessons.title: Stellar evolution compared: Sun-like stars and massive stars
lessons.bigQuestion: Will the Sun end with a bang or a whimper?
objectives: Describe the evolution of Sun-like stars from nebula to white dwarf
Describe the evolution of stars more massive than the Sun
Explain how mass decides a star's final stage
successCriteria: All: order the stages for a Sun-like star
Most: compare the end stages of the two types of star
Some: explain stability on the main sequence and the origin of heavier elements
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: origin of the elements; History: Islamic astronomers' observations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the life and end of stars

keywords.def: a cloud of dust and gas where stars form
long, stable stage where hydrogen fuses to helium in the core
large cool star after the core hydrogen is used up
explosion of a massive star at the end of its life

starter: Bismillah. State what force pulls a nebula together.
State what happens in the core of a main sequence star.
Define a galaxy.

teach.heading: Sun-like stars
bullets: Nebula: a cloud of gas and dust
Protostar forms as gravity pulls the cloud together
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses into helium
teach.note: Sequence: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf. Gravity pulls inwards; heat and radiation pressure from fusion push outwards; main sequence is stable because they balance. When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core contracts and the outer layers expand and cool (red giant). The outer layers drift off and the core remains as a hot dense white dwarf, which cools over time (approx. billions of years).

teach.heading: Massive stars
bullets: Same start: nebula, protostar, main sequence
Then expand to a red supergiant
Core collapses and a supernova explodes
Leaves a neutron star or black hole
teach.note: The spec points focus on the stages. Very massive stars create heavier elements by fusion, up to iron in the core, and the supernova spreads elements into space, which form new stars, planets and us. A neutron star is extremely dense; if the core is massive enough, a black hole forms (gravity so strong that not even light escapes).

teach.heading: Compare the paths
bullets: The mass of the star decides its fate
Both start with nebula, protostar, main sequence
Larger mass: shorter life on the main sequence
Heavier elements formed and spread in a supernova
teach.note: Ask: why do bigger stars live shorter lives? They use fuel much faster. Model answer below.

model.problem: Describe the differences between the life cycle of the Sun and a star much more massive than the Sun.
steps: Both begin as a nebula that collapses to a protostar and then a main sequence star
The Sun becomes a red giant; the massive star becomes a red supergiant
The Sun's outer layers drift away leaving a white dwarf
The massive star ends in a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole
model.answer: Mass decides the end stage: white dwarf for Sun-like stars; neutron star or black hole for much more massive stars.

teach.heading: Check: end stages
teach.note: Option A is the typical error of putting a black hole after any star. Option C is the wrong order.

check.q: Which is the final stage of a star like the Sun?
check.why: The Sun is not massive enough to become a supernova. It will end as a white dwarf.

practice: Put in order: red giant, nebula, main sequence, white dwarf, protostar.
State what balances gravity during the main sequence.
State two differences between the end of the Sun and a more massive star.
independent: Core: Draw a flow chart for the life cycle of the Sun.
Extend: Draw a flow chart for a massive star and compare the two.
Stretch: Explain why heavy elements on Earth came from earlier stars.
exit: State the stage after the main sequence for a Sun-like star.
State what may be left after a supernova.
Big question: how does the Sun end?
lessons.homework: Create a labelled life-cycle diagram of the Sun with a one-sentence explanation for each stage.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide stage cards for sorting with pictures. Stretch: explain why stable stars need a balance of forces.

lessons.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram
lessons.bigQuestion: If we plot every star by brightness and temperature, what pattern appears?
objectives: Draw the main components of the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram
Place main sequence stars, red giants and white dwarfs
Use the diagram to follow the life of a star
successCriteria: All: label the axes and the main groups
Most: place the Sun and describe star movements
Some: use the diagram to compare stars' luminosity, temperature and size
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: graphs with reversed axes; Astronomy
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: finding order in what looks random

keywords.def: total energy emitted per second by a star
temperature at a star's visible surface, in kelvin
band of stars in the H-R diagram where stars fuse hydrogen
small, hot, dim star

starter: Bismillah. State what makes a star hot.
Name the final stage of a Sun-like star.
State what colour hot stars appear.

teach.heading: The axes
bullets: Hot blue stars on the left; cool red on the right
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. The unusual axis, with temperature decreasing from left to right, is a historic convention. Luminosity is often a log scale, with the Sun at 1. Typical temperatures: the Sun's surface is about 5800 K (approx.; verify); hot blue stars exceed 10 000 K. Colour: hot blue-white, then yellow, then orange and red.

teach.heading: Groups of stars
bullets: Main sequence: diagonal band, top left to bottom right
Red giants and supergiants: top right
The Sun is in the middle of the main sequence
teach.note: Draw a sketch on the board. Red giants are cool but very luminous, so they must be very large. White dwarfs are hot but dim, so they must be very small. Most stars (about 90%, approx.) are on the main sequence. Stars move on the diagram as they evolve: from the main sequence to red giant, and then to the white dwarf region.
cycle: Moves up and right as a red giant
Core shrinks and outer layers lost
Ends in the white dwarf region

teach.heading: Draw the diagram
bullets: Mark red giants, supergiants and white dwarfs
teach.note: Pupils sketch their own. Marks usually go for correct axes (with temperature reversed), position of main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.

model.problem: Sketch an H-R diagram and explain the position of white dwarfs.
steps: Vertical axis luminosity, horizontal axis temperature decreasing to the right
Main sequence: band from top left to bottom right
Red giants: top right; white dwarfs: bottom left
White dwarfs are hot but have low luminosity, so they must be very small
model.answer: White dwarfs sit at bottom left: hot but small and dim.

teach.heading: Check: reading the diagram
teach.note: Option B confuses cool with hot. Option D reverses small and large.

check.q: A star is cool but has a high luminosity. Where is it on the H-R diagram?
check.why: Cool stars are on the right; high luminosity means near the top. They are red giants or supergiants and are very large.

practice: State the quantity on the vertical axis of the H-R diagram.
State where the Sun is found.
Describe the position of white dwarfs.
independent: Core: Sketch an H-R diagram with the main groups.
Extend: Mark the path of the Sun from main sequence to white dwarf.
Stretch: Explain why a cool star can have a high luminosity.
exit: Name the axes of the H-R diagram.
Name the region of the largest stars.
Big question: what pattern do stars make?
lessons.homework: Draw the H-R diagram on a poster and add three notes explaining why red giants and white dwarfs are where they are.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a template diagram to complete. Stretch: link luminosity, temperature and radius (beyond specification; verify).

lessons.title: Evolution of the universe and the case for the Big Bang
lessons.bigQuestion: What evidence tells us the universe had a beginning?
objectives: Describe the past evolution of the universe according to the Big Bang theory
State the evidence for the Big Bang: red-shift and the cosmic microwave background
Evaluate how well the evidence supports the theory
successCriteria: All: describe the Big Bang in a sentence
Most: explain how red-shift and the CMB support it
Some: evaluate the evidence and compare it with the steady-state theory
lessons.crossCurricular: History of science; Philosophy: evidence and belief
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the universe as a sign; scientific theories change as evidence changes

keywords.def: the universe began from a hot, dense state and has been expanding since
stretching of light from a receding galaxy to longer wavelengths
microwave radiation arriving from all directions in space
the increase in distance between galaxies

starter: Bismillah. Define red-shift.
State where microwaves come in the electromagnetic spectrum.
State what the Doppler effect is.

teach.heading: The Big Bang model
bullets: The universe began very small, hot and dense
It has expanded and cooled over time
Time began about 13.8 billion years ago (approx.; verify)
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. Avoid saying it was an explosion into empty space: space itself expands. Ask pupils to draw dots on a balloon, inflate, and watch the dots move apart; there is no centre. The age is approximately 13.8 billion years (verify the value used by the board).

timeline.label: Later
timeline.text: Matter clumps into stars and galaxies

teach.heading: Evidence 1: red-shift
bullets: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted
Galaxies are moving away from us
More distant galaxies show greater red-shift
teach.note: Link to the Doppler effect: waves from a receding source are stretched to longer wavelength. Extrapolating backwards in time, all matter was once together. Pupils must say 'more distant galaxies are moving away faster'. Do not imply that Earth is at the centre.

misconception.wrong: Red-shift shows that the Earth is at the centre of the universe.
misconception.right: Every distant galaxy sees others moving away, like dots on an inflating balloon. There is no centre.

teach.heading: Evidence 2: cosmic microwave background
bullets: Remnant of the hot early universe
Stretched to microwave wavelength by expansion
teach.note: The CMB is radiation released early in the universe's history. As space expanded the wavelength stretched from very short to the microwave region; today it corresponds to about 2.7 K (approx.; verify). The Big Bang predicted it before it was found. Competing steady-state theory could not explain it.

model.problem: Explain how red-shift and the CMB support the Big Bang theory.
steps: Red-shift: galaxies move away from us, so the universe is expanding
More distant galaxies move away faster, matching an expanding universe
Expansion backwards in time suggests a hot dense start
CMB: leftover radiation from the early hot universe, stretched to microwaves, seen from all directions
model.answer: Red-shift shows expansion and the CMB shows a hot early universe, both predicted by the Big Bang theory.

teach.heading: Check: evidence
teach.note: Option A would be blue-shift. Option D is a common wrong claim.

check.q: Light from a distant galaxy has a longer wavelength than expected. This shows the galaxy is...
check.why: Longer wavelength (red-shift) means the source is moving away from the observer.

teach.heading: Evaluating the theory
bullets: Theories change as new data arrives
teach.note: Discuss science as an ongoing process: theory, prediction, observation. Ask: what would make scientists change their minds? Link to respect for evidence and humility about what we do not know.

practice: State the evidence for an expanding universe.
Explain why the CMB is in the microwave region.
State why the Big Bang is not an explosion into empty space.
independent: Core: Make a timeline of the universe from the Big Bang to now.
Extend: Explain how red-shift evidence supports expansion.
Stretch: Evaluate how the CMB supports the Big Bang more strongly than red-shift alone.
exit: Name two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
State what red-shift shows.
Big question: what tells us the universe had a beginning?
lessons.homework: Write a balanced paragraph: 'the Big Bang theory is well supported by evidence'. Use at least two pieces of evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use the balloon model and a word bank. Stretch: discuss alternative theories and why they fell out of favour.
